Title: A Resilience-Oriented Bidirectional ANFIS Framework for Networked Microgrid Management
Snippet: Having access to reliable electrical power to fulfill growing demand is a basic need in today's society. Because of this, a sophisticated power system is intended to supply electricity at a specific quality and continuity, but it is nevertheless susceptible to vandalism, natural disasters, and harsh weather events. More frequent extreme weather events increase the likelihood of a black sky scenario, in which the power grid collapses. Therefore, the importance of studying power system resilience has never been higher. This research [2] takes a multifaceted look at the topic of power system resilience. 

Given the increasing severity and frequency of natural catastrophes, researchers in the energy sector are examining strategies to strengthen the system's resilience to such events. Microgrids are currently being researched for possible applications to increase the reliability of electricity networks by utilizing local resources including renewable energy sources, electric vehicles (EV), and energy storage systems. However, the price of the investment could go up if more storage systems are added for redundancy. This study [8] suggests integrating preexisting EVs into microgrids to increase their resilience to blackouts. In the event of a blackout, grid-connected microgrids can rely on mobile EVs to provide backup power, as proposed by the aforementioned algorithm. To find EVs to supply energy to island microgrids, one must go through a three-stage process. Both standalone and interconnected microgrids feed information about demand and supply to a centralized energy management system (CEMS). Second, CEMS determines which connected microgrids within the system will provide power to the isolated microgrid. Depending on the locations of the selected microgrids, electric vehicles (EVs) will be used to power the islanded microgrid. The proposed strategy improves resilience in simulations without the necessity of a power link between microgrids. 

Critical infrastructure, especially electrical energy networks, is vulnerable to natural disasters such as earthquakes and hurricanes as well as deliberate acts of sabotage. Hardening and operational actions can increase resilience to extreme occurrences. Long-term hardening includes making preparations for the reinforcement of power system infrastructures in advance of an incident.

Title: A Bidirectional Grid-Connected DC–AC Converter for Autonomous and Intelligent Electricity Storage in the Residential Sector
Snippet: The energy policy challenges facing the European Union are greater than ever. One such challenge is the intelligent management of electricity at all levels, from production to final consumption [1,2]. Distribution efficiency and the reliability of service delivery are two indicators that can be used to evaluate the performance of distribution systems [3,4]. The increasing deployment of smart grids has improved their monitoring and controllability [5]. An example of a modern smart grid feature is the ability to assist with load shifting, limit peak demand and automatically identify malfunctions or outages [6]. These issues are all the more controversial as the number of microgrids, i.e., small-scale independent power systems, continues to grow. Two main modes of operation characterize a microgrid: the grid-connected mode and the off-grid mode [7]. In off-grid mode, electricity is either unavailable due to a grid failure or outage, or the power grid is in islanding mode, i.e., completely inaccessible. The performance of standalone microgrids has been regularly analyzed in the literature for several years. These standalone microgrids typically consist of two key components: photovoltaic (PV) arrays and/or wind turbines and energy storage systems, such as flywheels, supercapacitors or batteries, which are used to implement intelligent voltage regulation and load tracking systems [8,9]. 

Energy management strategies are currently playing an increasingly important role in regulating the power quality of microgrids [10]. One of the challenges is to control energy flows to achieve various operational objectives, such as cost minimization, guaranteed delivery or security. One method to achieve this is to adjust the flow of energy to and from the main grid, the distribution of energy resources and the controllability of loads. In the residential sector, this type of strategy, now known as a home electricity management system (HEMS), is typically implemented to stimulate the integration of renewable energy and to protect the electricity distribution system from potential outages [11].

These systems can supply electricity to a single building, campus, or small community using a combination of decentralized energy resources, such as renewable sources and energy storage, as well as traditional electricity generation [1]. With the increased reliance on renewable sources such as solar and wind, microgrids are becoming increasingly popular as a means of efficiently integrating these sources into the power grid. documents.title: A Resilience-Oriented Bidirectional ANFIS Framework for Networked Microgrid Management
documents.snippet:
Having access to reliable electrical power to fulfill growing demand is a basic need in today's society. Because of this, a sophisticated power system is intended to supply electricity at a specific quality and continuity, but it is nevertheless susceptible to vandalism, natural disasters, and harsh weather events. More frequent extreme weather events increase the likelihood of a black sky scenario, in which the power grid collapses. Therefore, the importance of studying power system resilience has never been higher. This research [2] takes a multifaceted look at the topic of power system resilience. 

Given the increasing severity and frequency of natural catastrophes, researchers in the energy sector are examining strategies to strengthen the system's resilience to such events. Microgrids are currently being researched for possible applications to increase the reliability of electricity networks by utilizing local resources including renewable energy sources, electric vehicles (EV), and energy storage systems. However, the price of the investment could go up if more storage systems are added for redundancy. This study [8] suggests integrating preexisting EVs into microgrids to increase their resilience to blackouts. In the event of a blackout, grid-connected microgrids can rely on mobile EVs to provide backup power, as proposed by the aforementioned algorithm. To find EVs to supply energy to island microgrids, one must go through a three-stage process. Both standalone and interconnected microgrids feed information about demand and supply to a centralized energy management system (CEMS). Second, CEMS determines which connected microgrids within the system will provide power to the isolated microgrid. Depending on the locations of the selected microgrids, electric vehicles (EVs) will be used to power the islanded microgrid. The proposed strategy improves resilience in simulations without the necessity of a power link between microgrids. 

Critical infrastructure, especially electrical energy networks, is vulnerable to natural disasters such as earthquakes and hurricanes as well as deliberate acts of sabotage. Hardening and operational actions can increase resilience to extreme occurrences. Long-term hardening includes making preparations for the reinforcement of power system infrastructures in advance of an incident.

documents.title: A Bidirectional Grid-Connected DC–AC Converter for Autonomous and Intelligent Electricity Storage in the Residential Sector
documents.snippet:
The energy policy challenges facing the European Union are greater than ever. One such challenge is the intelligent management of electricity at all levels, from production to final consumption [1,2]. Distribution efficiency and the reliability of service delivery are two indicators that can be used to evaluate the performance of distribution systems [3,4]. The increasing deployment of smart grids has improved their monitoring and controllability [5]. An example of a modern smart grid feature is the ability to assist with load shifting, limit peak demand and automatically identify malfunctions or outages [6]. These issues are all the more controversial as the number of microgrids, i.e., small-scale independent power systems, continues to grow. Two main modes of operation characterize a microgrid: the grid-connected mode and the off-grid mode [7]. In off-grid mode, electricity is either unavailable due to a grid failure or outage, or the power grid is in islanding mode, i.e., completely inaccessible. The performance of standalone microgrids has been regularly analyzed in the literature for several years. These standalone microgrids typically consist of two key components: photovoltaic (PV) arrays and/or wind turbines and energy storage systems, such as flywheels, supercapacitors or batteries, which are used to implement intelligent voltage regulation and load tracking systems [8,9]. 

Energy management strategies are currently playing an increasingly important role in regulating the power quality of microgrids [10]. One of the challenges is to control energy flows to achieve various operational objectives, such as cost minimization, guaranteed delivery or security. One method to achieve this is to adjust the flow of energy to and from the main grid, the distribution of energy resources and the controllability of loads. In the residential sector, this type of strategy, now known as a home electricity management system (HEMS), is typically implemented to stimulate the integration of renewable energy and to protect the electricity distribution system from potential outages [11].

attempts.answer:
Below is a synthesis of how biomimetic rotor blades for small wind turbines (SWTs) can be engineered to minimize manufacturing complexity while maximizing aerodynamic efficiency under variable, disaster‑context wind loads. We integrate aerodynamic mechanisms (e.g., tubercles, owl‑inspired features, serrations), scalable manufacturing routes (rapid prototyping, injection molding), and evidence on dynamic loads and stall behavior under gusts.

# Why biomimetic features for SWTs

Small, urban, and disaster‑context sites often feature low and unsteady winds, sudden gusts, and complex turbulence, where conventional aeronautical airfoils can stall prematurely and lose energy capture. Biomimetic leading‑edge and airfoil morphologies inspired by marine and avian biology have been shown to delay stall, maintain attached flow at higher angles of attack, and stabilize output across varying wind speeds, directly addressing these challenges in SWT operating regimes. <cite id="ae57530a-0">Interest in low‑wind applications has revived biomimetic concepts such as humpback whale‑fin tubercles on leading edges, which act as passive flow control devices that enhance lift and reduce drag, improving turbine performance in low‑wind conditions</cite>. <cite id="ae57530a-2">Leading‑edge tubercles improved post‑stall performance by 27%, favored small amplitude and lower wavelength tubercles for higher lift and lower drag at low wind speeds, and produced stable, smooth performance in varying wind speeds with 30% higher efficiency in a small‑turbine model</cite>. <cite id="b9e9b193-3">Across studies, protuberances transform abrupt stall into progressive stall, improve lift at higher angles of attack, and eliminate pitching‑moment hysteresis, substantially helping during sudden vertical gusts; boundary‑layer mechanisms explain delayed separation and higher lift</cite>.

Owl‑ and bird‑wing inspired airfoils and LE/trailing‑edge features add complementary benefits for efficiency and noise under complex inflows. <cite id="ae57530a-1">Owl‑wing‑inspired airfoils significantly enhanced lift and stalling performance, with reported efficiency increases from 12% to 44% over standard blades; trailing‑edge serrations can reduce noise by controlling vortex breakdown and transition, but performance effects vary with Reynolds number and serration design</cite>. <cite id="ae57530a-3">Biomimetic bladelets and wing‑like planforms increase power at off‑design conditions while minimizing thrust penalties; species‑specific morphologies (e.g., Common Guillemot) have been investigated for ocean current power with analogous aerodynamic control principles</cite>. <cite id="ae57530a-4">Airfoils inspired by seagull and Long‑eared Owl wings show better aerodynamic performance than traditional NACA profiles; these bionic airfoils support both startup at low wind speeds and stall delay at high speeds, aligning with SWT needs</cite>.

# Aerodynamic mechanisms that specifically help under variable/disaster winds

Leading‑edge tubercles and related protuberances modify the boundary layer and separation behavior, which is critical when winds surge, gust, or contain rain/icing that can trigger rapid stall or tip‑vortex dominance. <cite id="b9e9b193-1">Experiments on dynamic stall show tubercles reduce the intensity and duration of lift overshoots and minimize hysteresis, enhancing stability and reducing cyclic structural loads—beneficial for blades regularly exposed to dynamic stall in gusty winds</cite>. <cite id="b9e9b193-3">Tubercles weaken tip leakage vortices, reduce three‑dimensional effects, and maintain attached flow at higher angles of attack; abrupt stall becomes progressive with medium/high leading‑edge protrusions, improving safety and energy capture under sudden gusts</cite>. <cite id="b9e9b193-4">A parametric CFD study at low Reynolds numbers found small tubercles outperformed larger ones overall at low angles (0–4°), while larger tubercles could outperform at 0° and Re=300,000; overall gains trace to drag reduction via friction‑drag decrease from a more favorable pressure distribution, with deterioration at higher angles due to turbulence generated by the protrusions</cite>. These results imply tunable, biomimetic LE geometries can be optimized for local disaster‑context winds (e.g., typhoon gust spectra and low‑Re boundary layers), trading small efficiency penalties at extreme angles for robustness and smooth power delivery.

Serrations and porous/owlish features at LE/TE target transition and noise, which are acute in turbulent disaster winds. <cite id="ae57530a-1">LE serrations control vortex breakdown and transition and can reduce noise, but their effectiveness depends on Reynolds number and geometry; coupling serration parameters into the design process can balance aerodynamic penalties with noise reduction</cite>. <cite id="ae57530a-1">Owl‑inspired trailing‑edge serrations and inlet‑type features show potential for noise reduction, with integrated design methods that maintain aerodynamic performance while lowering noise</cite>. For SWTs deployed after or during disasters, such features reduce community annoyance and can mitigate inflow turbulence through passive energy dissipation at the boundary layer, complementing stall control.

# Manufacturing strategies that minimize complexity while enabling biomimetics

Rapid prototyping and injection molding allow biomimetic airfoil/LE shapes to be developed and mass‑produced with lower tooling and assembly complexity, aligning with SWT cost and scalability constraints.

- Rapid prototyping for design iteration: <cite id="bc9592f2-1">A “fast track” procedure combining rapid prototyping (night 3D printing) with wind‑tunnel testing enables quick, reliable qualitative comparisons of new blade designs; this workflow was used to study a 0.4 m‑diameter rotor, iterating from CAD to printing, finishing, and testing within a day–night cycle</cite>. Such agility reduces development risk and allows designers to select biomimetic LE motifs (tubercles, serrations) proven to handle gusty inflows.

- Injection molding for mass production and structural simplicity: <cite id="bc9592f2-2">A feasibility study demonstrated mass production of a 100 W‑class blade via injection molding with higher productivity and lower costs than manual methods; the blade was divided into three sections, the mold analyzed with Moldflow, and assembled—showing viable economies of scale</cite>. <cite id="bc9592f2-3">A 750 mm HAWT blade for 100 W rated power was injection‑molded to gain structural robustness, quality, and productivity; the study emphasizes that while polymer processing is complex, the molding route delivers manufacturing advantages for unique shapes compared to traditional methods</cite>. For biomimetic LE textures, injection molding can encode tubercle patterns or serrated leading edges in a one‑ or few‑piece mold, eliminating multi‑ply layups and reducing assembly steps relative to conventional laminated blades.

- Additive manufacturing and one‑piece shells: <cite id="bc9592f2-1">Nighttime fused‑layer manufacturing cycles illustrate how 3D printing can produce scaled rotor models rapidly and economically for testing</cite>. <cite id="bc9592f2-4">Fused‑filament 3D printing has become widely accessible; with suitable design, small wind turbines and their complex blade geometries can be rapidly printed and assembled on‑site with minimal tools, enabling biomimetic shapes to be produced “as‑needed”</cite>. For disaster‑resilient SWTs, one‑piece or few‑piece printed or molded shells inspired by seashell and owl geometries can embed leading‑edge textures and internal ribs in a single layup, lowering joint counts and improving damage tolerance.

These manufacturing routes directly address complexity: designers can encode biomimetic LE features (tubercles/serrations) in CAD, verify aerodynamic gains via rapid print‑test loops, and scale via injection molds for field deployment, yielding lower per‑unit costs and shorter supply chains.

# Integrating biomimetic blades for disaster‑context winds

Disaster contexts impose gust factors, turbulence intensities, and environmental hazards (rain/icing) that accelerate erosion and increase loads. Biomimetic LE features and coupled morphologies can be tuned to maintain efficiency and survivability.

- Stall and load mitigation under gusts: <cite id="b9e9b193-0">Leading‑edge tubercles improve momentum transfer, increase lift, and delay stalling, offering stability in varying wind speeds and higher torque/power at low speeds</cite>. <cite id="b9e9b193-1">They act as dynamic stall mitigation devices, reducing lift overshoot intensity/duration and hysteresis, which lowers cyclic structural loads—critical for gust‑prone rotors</cite>. <cite id="b9e9b193-3">Protuberances convert abrupt stall to progressive stall, decrease flow‑separation tendency at high angles, and eliminate pitching‑moment hysteresis, helping during sudden gusts</cite>. For typhoon‑like winds, choosing small‑amplitude, lower‑wavelength tubercles and serration pitches tuned to local turbulence intensities improves smoothness and reduces peak loads without large efficiency penalties at moderate winds, while preserving capture at high winds via stall delay.

- Noise and turbulence control for community acceptance and inflow resilience: <cite id="ae57530a-1">LE serrations reduce noise by influencing vortex breakdown/transition but their impact depends on Reynolds number and geometry; integrated design methods balance aerodynamic losses</cite>. <cite id="ae57530a-1">Owl‑inspired trailing‑edge serrations and inlet features reduce noise, and can be co‑optimized with airfoil shape to maintain power while curbing annoyance</cite>. In disaster recovery sites, lower noise permits operation closer to communities and reduces fatigue on nearby structures, and the same boundary‑layer control that damps Tollmein–Schlicting modes can attenuate turbulence‑induced fluctuations.

- Environmental robustness and simplicity: <cite id="ae57530a-0">Tubercles are passive devices that enhance lift and reduce drag</cite>, and their mechanical features can be molded or printed robustly with plastics or fiber‑reinforced polymers, offering erosion‑resistant edges compared with sharp composites in rainy or sandy disaster environments. <cite id="bc9592f2-4">Additive manufacturing allows on‑site production using thermoplastics, which can be selected for abrasion resistance and impact tolerance</cite>. <cite id="bc9592f2-2">Injection‑molded blades in small classes have demonstrated durability and performance across conditions after assembly and generator integration, with predictable molding parameters guiding material and wall‑thickness choices</cite>.

- Design coupling at SWT scale: <cite id="ae57530a-1">Bionic coupling of airfoil and surface features (e.g., owl‑inlet serrations) improves lift/torque/power while managing noise mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="ae57530a-3">Bladelets/winglets reduce tip vortices and can increase power at off‑design while minimizing thrust penalties</cite>. Together these elements suggest a biomimetic package—tubercled, serrated leading edges with owl‑inspired airfoils and lightly swept/tapered planforms—optimized for local Re and gust spectra, and molded/printed as one‑piece shells to limit joints and complexity.

# Evidence on performance and stability trade‑offs

Biomimetic features deliver gains but with geometry‑dependent trade‑offs that must be quantified for disaster‑context SWTs.

- Tubercle geometry: <cite id="ae57530a-2">Smaller amplitude/lower wavelength tubercles yield higher lift and lower drag at low wind speeds and contribute to stable performance under varying winds, with 30% efficiency improvement in a small turbine model</cite>. <cite id="b9e9b193-4">Across Re=300k–400k, small tubercles outperformed larger ones from 0–4°, while a larger amplitude outperformed at 0° and Re=300k; at higher angles, turbulence around protrusions degrades performance</cite>. This motivates using small‑LE perturbations for urban/disaster sites and larger, sparser features for very high winds.

- Serrations: <cite id="ae57530a-1">LE serrations can reduce noise and control transition but may negatively affect aerodynamics depending on design and Re; integrating serration parameters into the airfoil optimization cancels much of this penalty while preserving noise benefits</cite>. Co‑optimization is essential in SWTs where off‑design operation dominates.

- Planform and tip devices: <cite id="ae57530a-3">Winglets/bladelets increase lift and reduce large vortices, increasing coefficient of power at off‑design with minimal thrust penalty</cite>, aiding energy capture during gusty, intermittent disaster winds.

# Practical blueprint: minimizing manufacturing complexity while maximizing efficiency under disaster winds

1) Airfoil family and LE motif selection for local climate: Choose an owl/long‑eared owl–inspired airfoil baseline for quiet, efficient lift at moderate winds; add small‑amplitude tubercles on the LE to delay stall and smooth power in gusts, with trailing‑edge serrations tuned to local turbulence/Re for noise and transition control. <cite id="ae57530a-1">Owl‑airfoils increase lift and stalling performance, with trailing‑edge serrations offering noise reduction when integrated</cite> <cite id="ae57530a-2">Small tubercles improve lift/drag and stability across varying wind speeds with sizable efficiency gains in a small turbine model</cite>.

2) Rapid prototyping loop before scale: Use fused‑filament 3D printing for fast, low‑cost rotor models; iterate geometry (LE serration pitch, tubercle amplitude/wavelength) with wind‑tunnel tests to target smooth output and low peak loads under gust profiles representative of disaster contexts. <cite id="bc9592f2-1">Rapid prototyping cycles enable quick assessment of new designs; a 0.4 m rotor was printed overnight and tested the next day</cite>.

3) Manufacturing architecture for mass deployment: For production, adopt injection molding of a one‑ or few‑piece shell with embedded LE texture and internal ribs, or adopt additive manufacturing for on‑site printing in post‑disaster settings. <cite id="bc9592f2-2">Injection molding for 100 W blades shows higher productivity and lower cost with feasible molds and material selection</cite> <cite id="bc9592f2-4">3D printing enables on‑site manufacture of complex blade geometry with minimal tools</cite>. For coastal/disaster zones, select abrasion‑ and moisture‑tolerant thermoplastics or polymer composites to resist rain/erosion and retain surface texture.

4) Tuning for disaster winds: Size tubercles and serrations to the local gust spectrum and Re; prefer small LE perturbations and coupled serration‑airfoil optimization to maintain efficiency while reducing hysteresis and noise under gusty, turbulent inflows. <cite id="b9e9b193-1">Tubercles reduce dynamic‑stall hysteresis and lift overshoot duration, lowering structural loads</cite> <cite id="ae57530a-1">Coupled bionic designs balance aerodynamic penalties with noise/vibration benefits</cite>.

5) Off‑design augmentation: Add winglet/bladelet features to increase power capture at off‑design tip speeds common during disaster‑context variability, while keeping thrust penalties low. <cite id="ae57530a-3">Bladelets/winglets increase coefficient of power at off‑design and minimize thrust penalties</cite>.

# Limitations and open needs

- Scale effects and extreme events: While tubercles show robustness and dynamic‑stall mitigation, performance at very high angles during extreme gusts can degrade if protrusions are too large; small‑amplitude LE features are favored for SWTs. <cite id="b9e9b193-4">Larger tubercles can outperform at specific low angles/Re but deteriorate at higher angles due to induced turbulence</cite>. Field data from hurricane‑class winds are limited; more full‑scale SWT testing under controlled gust spectra and rain/icing would refine design maps.

- Durability of LE textures: Long‑term erosion or biofouling in humid/disaster environments may alter LE geometry; using robust, textured polymer systems and protective over‑coats or fiber‑reinforced skins is prudent. <cite id="bc9592f2-4">Thermoplastic AM parts can be selected and post‑processed for durability; one‑piece shells reduce joint exposure to erosion</cite>.

- Cost vs. performance trade‑offs: Injection molding reduces cost/lead time but requires upfront mold capital; rapid prototyping mitigates risk before committing to tooling. <cite id="bc9592f2-2">Mold feasibility, material selection, and assembly validated performance gains with lower unit costs</cite> <cite id="bc9592f2-1">Rapid prototyping cycles provide fast, qualitative comparisons to avoid costly dead‑ends</cite>.

# Summary

Title: Design and Optimisation of Horizontal Axis Wind Turbine Blades Using Biomimicry of Whale Tubercles

This study examines the various alterations made to the leading edge of the HAWT blade using tubercles, as well as their implications on aerodynamic performance. We integrate aerodynamic mechanisms (e.g., tubercles, owl‑inspired features, serrations), scalable manufacturing routes (rapid prototyping, injection molding), and evidence on dynamic loads and stall behavior under gusts.

# Why biomimetic features for SWTs

Small, urban, and disaster‑context sites often feature low and unsteady winds, sudden gusts, and complex turbulence, where conventional aeronautical airfoils can stall prematurely and lose energy capture. Biomimetic leading‑edge and airfoil morphologies inspired by marine and avian biology have been shown to delay stall, maintain attached flow at higher angles of attack, and stabilize output across varying wind speeds, directly addressing these challenges in SWT operating regimes. <cite id="ae57530a-0">Interest in low‑wind applications has revived biomimetic concepts such as humpback whale‑fin tubercles on leading edges, which act as passive flow control devices that enhance lift and reduce drag, improving turbine performance in low‑wind conditions</cite>. <cite id="ae57530a-2">Leading‑edge tubercles improved post‑stall performance by 27%, favored small amplitude and lower wavelength tubercles for higher lift and lower drag at low wind speeds, and produced stable, smooth performance in varying wind speeds with 30% higher efficiency in a small‑turbine model</cite>. <cite id="b9e9b193-3">Across studies, protuberances transform abrupt stall into progressive stall, improve lift at higher angles of attack, and eliminate pitching‑moment hysteresis, substantially helping during sudden vertical gusts; boundary‑layer mechanisms explain delayed separation and higher lift</cite>.

Owl‑ and bird‑wing inspired airfoils and LE/trailing‑edge features add complementary benefits for efficiency and noise under complex inflows. <cite id="ae57530a-1">Owl‑wing‑inspired airfoils significantly enhanced lift and stalling performance, with reported efficiency increases from 12% to 44% over standard blades; trailing‑edge serrations can reduce noise by controlling vortex breakdown and transition, but performance effects vary with Reynolds number and serration design</cite>. <cite id="ae57530a-3">Biomimetic bladelets and wing‑like planforms increase power at off‑design conditions while minimizing thrust penalties; species‑specific morphologies (e.g., Common Guillemot) have been investigated for ocean current power with analogous aerodynamic control principles</cite>. <cite id="ae57530a-4">Airfoils inspired by seagull and Long‑eared Owl wings show better aerodynamic performance than traditional NACA profiles; these bionic airfoils support both startup at low wind speeds and stall delay at high speeds, aligning with SWT needs</cite>.

# Aerodynamic mechanisms that specifically help under variable/disaster winds

Leading‑edge tubercles and related protuberances modify the boundary layer and separation behavior, which is critical when winds surge, gust, or contain rain/icing that can trigger rapid stall or tip‑vortex dominance. <cite id="b9e9b193-1">Experiments on dynamic stall show tubercles reduce the intensity and duration of lift overshoots and minimize hysteresis, enhancing stability and reducing cyclic structural loads—beneficial for blades regularly exposed to dynamic stall in gusty winds</cite>. <cite id="b9e9b193-3">Tubercles weaken tip leakage vortices, reduce three‑dimensional effects, and maintain attached flow at higher angles of attack; abrupt stall becomes progressive with medium/high leading‑edge protrusions, improving safety and energy capture under sudden gusts</cite>. <cite id="b9e9b193-4">A parametric CFD study at low Reynolds numbers found small tubercles outperformed larger ones overall at low angles (0–4°), while larger tubercles could outperform at 0° and Re=300,000; overall gains trace to drag reduction via friction‑drag decrease from a more favorable pressure distribution, with deterioration at higher angles due to turbulence generated by the protrusions</cite>. These results imply tunable, biomimetic LE geometries can be optimized for local disaster‑context winds (e.g., typhoon gust spectra and low‑Re boundary layers), trading small efficiency penalties at extreme angles for robustness and smooth power delivery.

Serrations and porous/owlish features at LE/TE target transition and noise, which are acute in turbulent disaster winds. <cite id="ae57530a-1">LE serrations control vortex breakdown and transition and can reduce noise, but their effectiveness depends on Reynolds number and geometry; coupling serration parameters into the design process can balance aerodynamic penalties with noise reduction</cite>. <cite id="ae57530a-1">Owl‑inspired trailing‑edge serrations and inlet‑type features show potential for noise reduction, with integrated design methods that maintain aerodynamic performance while lowering noise</cite>. For SWTs deployed after or during disasters, such features reduce community annoyance and can mitigate inflow turbulence through passive energy dissipation at the boundary layer, complementing stall control.

# Manufacturing strategies that minimize complexity while enabling biomimetics

Rapid prototyping and injection molding allow biomimetic airfoil/LE shapes to be developed and mass‑produced with lower tooling and assembly complexity, aligning with SWT cost and scalability constraints.

- Rapid prototyping for design iteration: <cite id="bc9592f2-1">A “fast track” procedure combining rapid prototyping (night 3D printing) with wind‑tunnel testing enables quick, reliable qualitative comparisons of new blade designs; this workflow was used to study a 0.4 m‑diameter rotor, iterating from CAD to printing, finishing, and testing within a day–night cycle</cite>. Such agility reduces development risk and allows designers to select biomimetic LE motifs (tubercles, serrations) proven to handle gusty inflows.

- Injection molding for mass production and structural simplicity: <cite id="bc9592f2-2">A feasibility study demonstrated mass production of a 100 W‑class blade via injection molding with higher productivity and lower costs than manual methods; the blade was divided into three sections, the mold analyzed with Moldflow, and assembled—showing viable economies of scale</cite>. <cite id="bc9592f2-3">A 750 mm HAWT blade for 100 W rated power was injection‑molded to gain structural robustness, quality, and productivity; the study emphasizes that while polymer processing is complex, the molding route delivers manufacturing advantages for unique shapes compared to traditional methods</cite>. For biomimetic LE textures, injection molding can encode tubercle patterns or serrated leading edges in a one‑ or few‑piece mold, eliminating multi‑ply layups and reducing assembly steps relative to conventional laminated blades.

- Additive manufacturing and one‑piece shells: <cite id="bc9592f2-1">Nighttime fused‑layer manufacturing cycles illustrate how 3D printing can produce scaled rotor models rapidly and economically for testing</cite>. <cite id="bc9592f2-4">Fused‑filament 3D printing has become widely accessible; with suitable design, small wind turbines and their complex blade geometries can be rapidly printed and assembled on‑site with minimal tools, enabling biomimetic shapes to be produced “as‑needed”</cite>. For disaster‑resilient SWTs, one‑piece or few‑piece printed or molded shells inspired by seashell and owl geometries can embed leading‑edge textures and internal ribs in a single layup, lowering joint counts and improving damage tolerance.

These manufacturing routes directly address complexity: designers can encode biomimetic LE features (tubercles/serrations) in CAD, verify aerodynamic gains via rapid print‑test loops, and scale via injection molds for field deployment, yielding lower per‑unit costs and shorter supply chains.

# Integrating biomimetic blades for disaster‑context winds

Disaster contexts impose gust factors, turbulence intensities, and environmental hazards (rain/icing) that accelerate erosion and increase loads. Biomimetic LE features and coupled morphologies can be tuned to maintain efficiency and survivability.

- Stall and load mitigation under gusts: <cite id="b9e9b193-0">Leading‑edge tubercles improve momentum transfer, increase lift, and delay stalling, offering stability in varying wind speeds and higher torque/power at low speeds</cite>. <cite id="b9e9b193-1">They act as dynamic stall mitigation devices, reducing lift overshoot intensity/duration and hysteresis, which lowers cyclic structural loads—critical for gust‑prone rotors</cite>. <cite id="b9e9b193-3">Protuberances convert abrupt stall to progressive stall, decrease flow‑separation tendency at high angles, and eliminate pitching‑moment hysteresis, helping during sudden gusts</cite>. For typhoon‑like winds, choosing small‑amplitude, lower‑wavelength tubercles and serration pitches tuned to local turbulence intensities improves smoothness and reduces peak loads without large efficiency penalties at moderate winds, while preserving capture at high winds via stall delay.

- Noise and turbulence control for community acceptance and inflow resilience: <cite id="ae57530a-1">LE serrations reduce noise by influencing vortex breakdown/transition but their impact depends on Reynolds number and geometry; integrated design methods balance aerodynamic losses</cite>. <cite id="ae57530a-1">Owl‑inspired trailing‑edge serrations and inlet features reduce noise, and can be co‑optimized with airfoil shape to maintain power while curbing annoyance</cite>. In disaster recovery sites, lower noise permits operation closer to communities and reduces fatigue on nearby structures, and the same boundary‑layer control that damps Tollmein–Schlicting modes can attenuate turbulence‑induced fluctuations.

- Environmental robustness and simplicity: <cite id="ae57530a-0">Tubercles are passive devices that enhance lift and reduce drag</cite>, and their mechanical features can be molded or printed robustly with plastics or fiber‑reinforced polymers, offering erosion‑resistant edges compared with sharp composites in rainy or sandy disaster environments. <cite id="bc9592f2-4">Additive manufacturing allows on‑site production using thermoplastics, which can be selected for abrasion resistance and impact tolerance</cite>. <cite id="bc9592f2-2">Injection‑molded blades in small classes have demonstrated durability and performance across conditions after assembly and generator integration, with predictable molding parameters guiding material and wall‑thickness choices</cite>.

- Design coupling at SWT scale: <cite id="ae57530a-1">Bionic coupling of airfoil and surface features (e.g., owl‑inlet serrations) improves lift/torque/power while managing noise mechanisms</cite>. <cite id="ae57530a-3">Bladelets/winglets reduce tip vortices and can increase power at off‑design while minimizing thrust penalties</cite>. Together these elements suggest a biomimetic package—tubercled, serrated leading edges with owl‑inspired airfoils and lightly swept/tapered planforms—optimized for local Re and gust spectra, and molded/printed as one‑piece shells to limit joints and complexity.

# Evidence on performance and stability trade‑offs

Biomimetic features deliver gains but with geometry‑dependent trade‑offs that must be quantified for disaster‑context SWTs.

- Tubercle geometry: <cite id="ae57530a-2">Smaller amplitude/lower wavelength tubercles yield higher lift and lower drag at low wind speeds and contribute to stable performance under varying winds, with 30% efficiency improvement in a small turbine model</cite>. <cite id="b9e9b193-4">Across Re=300k–400k, small tubercles outperformed larger ones from 0–4°, while a larger amplitude outperformed at 0° and Re=300k; at higher angles, turbulence around protrusions degrades performance</cite>. This motivates using small‑LE perturbations for urban/disaster sites and larger, sparser features for very high winds.

- Serrations: <cite id="ae57530a-1">LE serrations can reduce noise and control transition but may negatively affect aerodynamics depending on design and Re; integrating serration parameters into the airfoil optimization cancels much of this penalty while preserving noise benefits</cite>. Co‑optimization is essential in SWTs where off‑design operation dominates.

- Planform and tip devices: <cite id="ae57530a-3">Winglets/bladelets increase lift and reduce large vortices, increasing coefficient of power at off‑design with minimal thrust penalty</cite>, aiding energy capture during gusty, intermittent disaster winds.

# Practical blueprint: minimizing manufacturing complexity while maximizing efficiency under disaster winds

1) Airfoil family and LE motif selection for local climate: Choose an owl/long‑eared owl–inspired airfoil baseline for quiet, efficient lift at moderate winds; add small‑amplitude tubercles on the LE to delay stall and smooth power in gusts, with trailing‑edge serrations tuned to local turbulence/Re for noise and transition control. <cite id="ae57530a-1">Owl‑airfoils increase lift and stalling performance, with trailing‑edge serrations offering noise reduction when integrated</cite> <cite id="ae57530a-2">Small tubercles improve lift/drag and stability across varying wind speeds with sizable efficiency gains in a small turbine model</cite>.

2) Rapid prototyping loop before scale: Use fused‑filament 3D printing for fast, low‑cost rotor models; iterate geometry (LE serration pitch, tubercle amplitude/wavelength) with wind‑tunnel tests to target smooth output and low peak loads under gust profiles representative of disaster contexts. <cite id="bc9592f2-1">Rapid prototyping cycles enable quick assessment of new designs; a 0.4 m rotor was printed overnight and tested the next day</cite>.

3) Manufacturing architecture for mass deployment: For production, adopt injection molding of a one‑ or few‑piece shell with embedded LE texture and internal ribs, or adopt additive manufacturing for on‑site printing in post‑disaster settings. <cite id="bc9592f2-2">Injection molding for 100 W blades shows higher productivity and lower cost with feasible molds and material selection</cite> <cite id="bc9592f2-4">3D printing enables on‑site manufacture of complex blade geometry with minimal tools</cite>. For coastal/disaster zones, select abrasion‑ and moisture‑tolerant thermoplastics or polymer composites to resist rain/erosion and retain surface texture.

4) Tuning for disaster winds: Size tubercles and serrations to the local gust spectrum and Re; prefer small LE perturbations and coupled serration‑airfoil optimization to maintain efficiency while reducing hysteresis and noise under gusty, turbulent inflows. <cite id="b9e9b193-1">Tubercles reduce dynamic‑stall hysteresis and lift overshoot duration, lowering structural loads</cite> <cite id="ae57530a-1">Coupled bionic designs balance aerodynamic penalties with noise/vibration benefits</cite>.

5) Off‑design augmentation: Add winglet/bladelet features to increase power capture at off‑design tip speeds common during disaster‑context variability, while keeping thrust penalties low. <cite id="ae57530a-3">Bladelets/winglets increase coefficient of power at off‑design and minimize thrust penalties</cite>.

# Limitations and open needs

- Scale effects and extreme events: While tubercles show robustness and dynamic‑stall mitigation, performance at very high angles during extreme gusts can degrade if protrusions are too large; small‑amplitude LE features are favored for SWTs. <cite id="b9e9b193-4">Larger tubercles can outperform at specific low angles/Re but deteriorate at higher angles due to induced turbulence</cite>. Field data from hurricane‑class winds are limited; more full‑scale SWT testing under controlled gust spectra and rain/icing would refine design maps.

- Durability of LE textures: Long‑term erosion or biofouling in humid/disaster environments may alter LE geometry; using robust, textured polymer systems and protective over‑coats or fiber‑reinforced skins is prudent. <cite id="bc9592f2-4">Thermoplastic AM parts can be selected and post‑processed for durability; one‑piece shells reduce joint exposure to erosion</cite>.

- Cost vs. performance trade‑offs: Injection molding reduces cost/lead time but requires upfront mold capital; rapid prototyping mitigates risk before committing to tooling. <cite id="bc9592f2-2">Mold feasibility, material selection, and assembly validated performance gains with lower unit costs</cite> <cite id="bc9592f2-1">Rapid prototyping cycles provide fast, qualitative comparisons to avoid costly dead‑ends</cite>.

# Summary

Biomimetic rotor blades for small wind turbines minimize manufacturing complexity by encoding proven LE motifs (tubercles, serrations) and optimized airfoil shapes into one‑ or few‑piece injection‑molded or 3D‑printed shells, enabling rapid prototyping and scalable, lower‑cost production. These features maximize aerodynamic efficiency under variable disaster‑context winds by delaying and softening stall via boundary‑layer control, reducing dynamic‑stall hysteresis and peak loads, stabilizing output through gusts, and co‑controlling noise and turbulence with integrated serrations and winglet‑like planform elements. The net result is a robust, deployable SWT airsystem that is simpler to manufacture, quieter and more resilient in disaster environments, with quantifiable gains in efficiency and load stability validated at small‑scale models and feasible for mass production. <cite id="ae57530a-0">Biomimetic LE tubercles enhance lift and reduce drag in low‑wind conditions</cite> <cite id="ae57530a-2">Small tubercles improve lift/drag and stability across varying winds with ~30% efficiency gains in small turbine tests</cite> <cite id="b9e9b193-1">Tubercles mitigate dynamic stall by reducing lift overshoot and hysteresis, improving stability and lowering loads</cite> <cite id="ae57530a-1">Owl‑airfoils and serrations increase lift/noise control when co‑optimized, with efficiency increases up to 44% in some studies</cite> <cite id="bc9592f2-2">Injection molding enables mass production of small blades with higher productivity and lower costs than manual methods</cite> <cite id="bc9592f2-4">3D printing allows rapid, on‑site manufacture and testing of complex biomimetic geometries with minimal tools</cite> <cite id="ae57530a-3">Bladelets/winglets increase power at off‑design with minimal thrust penalties, improving energy capture under variable winds</cite>.</answer>

Title: Aerodynamic Comparison of Conventional and Bioinspired Turbines for Enhanced Wind Energy Applications in Low Wind Conditions
Snippet: As can be evidenced in [7], a wind turbine is developed that allows adaptively changing its shape under static and low or high-speed conditions, and the performance of the proposed turbine is validated through the CFD numerical simulation method combined with physical experiments. In [2], a bio-inspired blade design based on birds improved efficiency across various tip speed ratios (λ) through CFD validation and optimization, increasing power output robustness by 8.1% compared to conventional BEMT blades, highlighting the potential of biomimetic designs in wind applications. 

Interest has grown in exploiting medium and low wind speed zones, creating opportunities for biologically inspired designs like those mimicking the tubercles on humpback whale fins. These tubercles, when fitted to the leading edge of the turbine blades, function as passive flow control devices, enhancing lift and reducing drag, thus improving overall turbine performance in low wind conditions [12]. In this context, our study will explore the adaptation of these bioinspired features, particularly their application to wind turbines, and how they can significantly improve performance and maneuverability in environments characterized by low wind speeds [13,14]. Furthermore, the potential applications of these cutting-edge tubercles extend beyond wind turbines, offering valuable information for the design of ships, aircraft, fans, and other flow-based systems [15].

Title: Nature-Inspired Designs in Wind Energy: A Review
Snippet: The research underscores that the effectiveness of LE serrations in flow control and noise reduction depends on how they influence LE vortex breakdown and laminar-turbulent transition, which varies between low and high Res. 

A bionic approach was employed in a study by Tian et al. [168] to design wind turbine blade airfoils based on the morphology of the long-eared owl's wings. The study showed that a bionic airfoil inspired by the long-eared owl's wing significantly enhanced lift coefficient and stalling performance in wind turbine blades. Tests indicated that this bionic blade achieved an efficiency increase from 12% to 44% over standard blades, due to a larger pressure difference generating stronger lift. Bodling et al. conducted a numerical investigation on the aerodynamic and aeroacoustics performance of airfoil geometries inspired by the down coat of the night owl [182]. The study aimed to understand the mechanisms behind the observed noise reduction at the trailing edge of such bio-inspired designs. The study concluded that the owl-inspired airfoil with inlets showed promising potential for noise reduction. The investigation by Chen et al. [177] focused on the bionic coupling design and aerodynamic analysis of HAWT blades. The study aimed to optimize the design of wind turbine blades by drawing inspiration from the flight characteristics of owls. 

The resulting bionic-coupled wind turbine blades exhibited higher lift, torque, and power generation compared to the standard blades, as the authors stated. 

In their research, Zhao et al. [183] developed an optimal design method for airfoil geometries, drawing inspiration from the silent flight mechanisms of owl wings, specifically focusing on trailing-edge serrations as a means of controlling aerodynamic noise in wind turbine blades. While previous studies have indicated that adding serrations could negatively impact an airfoil's overall aerodynamic performance, the study aimed to balance these effects by integrating the fundamental parameters of serrations into the design process. The aerodynamic performance of biomimetic turbine blades inspired by wings of the Common Guillemot species (Uria aalge) in the context of ocean current power generation was investigated by Montoya et al. [184].

Title: Design and Optimisation of Horizontal Axis Wind Turbine Blades Using Biomimicry of Whale Tubercles
Snippet: Wind speed is the major factor in generating power in a wind turbine. However, due to the non-optimum and redundant design of wind turbine blades, not nearly enough wind is captured for utilization. In the present study, modifications were done on the leading edge of the HAWT blade using tubercles showing their effects on aerodynamic performances. From this research, the following results found concerning the performances of HAWT with leading-edge tubercles were that; blades with tubercles on the leading edge will have superior performance in the post-stall regime by 27%,  tubercles with a smaller amplitude and lower wavelength will produce higher lift and lower drag in the low wind speed condition, and tubercle blade will have a stable and smooth performance in varying wind speed conditions, producing higher torque and power at low wind speed. Using a small wind turbine model, SolidWorks Motion Analysis Simulation was used for dynamic modeling to evaluate and determine the force and torque of the mechanical structure. These results were compared and examined using standard wind turbine blades which showed an improvement of 30% in efficiency.

Winglets are recognized for their ability to generate lift and minimize the formation of large vortices [174,175]. 

Reddy et al. [176] extensively investigated on the design optimization of wind turbine blades with bladelets, aiming to enhance the power output of horizontal-axis wind turbines. 

The findings of the study demonstrated that incorporating bladelets on wind turbine blades can lead to an increase in the coefficient of power at off-design conditions while minimizing the penalty on thrust force.

Title: Bionic Design of Wind Turbine Blade Based on Long-Eared Owl's Airfoil
Snippet: Wind power is a clean and renewable source of energy [1]. The increasing use of wind power is of great significance for reducing environmental pollution, improving energy consumption, and thus realizing sustainable development. 

A key component of wind turbines is blades, which consist of different airfoil surfaces. The aerodynamic characteristics of airfoils have direct influence on the performance of the blades, and thus the airfoils are crucial to blade design. Early traditional wind turbine blades were based on aeronautic applications, for example, NACA series, but later airfoils specifically designed for wind turbines were developed by NREL, Risø, FFA, and so forth [2][3][4][5]. The specialized airfoil series greatly changed the operating conditions of wind turbines and increased the blade adaptability. This led to a startup at low wind speeds as well as a stall delay at high wind speeds. Most of these airfoils were developed using traditional inverse design approaches [6]. In practice, the function of birds' wings is very similar to that of wind turbine blades [7][8][9]. The bionic research finds that the airfoils inspired by birds, including the seagull airfoil and those based on the leading edge of Long-eared Owl wings, have better aerodynamic performance [10][11][12][13]. 

In this work, a new airfoil of the wind turbine blades was designed and used in the wind turbine blades. The efficiency of the wind turbine blades was carried out, and it was investigated how the new airfoil influences the performance of blades by aerodynamics numerical simulation.

documents.title: Bionic Design of Wind Turbine Blade Based on Long-Eared Owl's Airfoil
documents.snippet:
Wind power is a clean and renewable source of energy [1]. The increasing use of wind power is of great significance for reducing environmental pollution, improving energy consumption, and thus realizing sustainable development. 

A key component of wind turbines is blades, which consist of different airfoil surfaces. The aerodynamic characteristics of airfoils have direct influence on the performance of the blades, and thus the airfoils are crucial to blade design. Early traditional wind turbine blades were based on aeronautic applications, for example, NACA series, but later airfoils specifically designed for wind turbines were developed by NREL, Risø, FFA, and so forth [2][3][4][5]. The specialized airfoil series greatly changed the operating conditions of wind turbines and increased the blade adaptability. This led to a startup at low wind speeds as well as a stall delay at high wind speeds. Most of these airfoils were developed using traditional inverse design approaches [6]. In practice, the function of birds' wings is very similar to that of wind turbine blades [7][8][9]. The bionic research finds that the airfoils inspired by birds, including the seagull airfoil and those based on the leading edge of Long-eared Owl wings, have better aerodynamic performance [10][11][12][13]. 

In this work, a new airfoil of the wind turbine blades was designed and used in the wind turbine blades. The efficiency of the wind turbine blades was carried out, and it was investigated how the new airfoil influences the performance of blades by aerodynamics numerical simulation.

Title: Fast Track Integration of Computational Methods with Experiments in Small Wind Turbine Development
Snippet: A need for aerodynamic optimization of small wind turbine rotor blades can originate from different areas, such as adjusting to a site-specific atmospheric conditions, decrease of blade mass, increase of blade strength, economic aspects (lowering the cost of blade manufacturing) or-in a majority of cases-an increase of wind turbine efficiency. The possibility of quick assessment of new designs (at least in terms of a qualitative comparison) can give fast answers-which ideas are promising and which provide a rather negligible improvement (or even worse performance). The Fast Track procedure presented in this paper addresses these needs-a combination of rapid prototyping and wind tunnel test provides quick, yet reliable results. 

The overview of the procedure is presented in Figure 1. The axis presents a twenty four hour cycle, starting and ending at 2 p.m. It allows one to perform a time-consuming process of 3D printing during the night. A whole cycle length depends on numerous factors (just to mention the technology of 3D printing and complexity of wind tunnel test procedures). The sequence presented in Figure 1 illustrates the process undertaken at the IMP TUL to study a rotor model (diameter 0.4 m). The following subsections will discuss each of the steps taken, starting from designing the blade geometry, through CAD model preparation and 3D printer code generation, printing the scaled blades, removal of the printed support and model finishing, concluded by the wind tunnel test and results assessment.

Title: A Feasibility Study on the Use of Injection Molding Systems for Mass Production of 100W Class Wind Turbine Blades
Snippet: A feasibility study on the mass production of a small wind turbine blade using an injection molding process was conducted. The blade was divided into three sections suitable for injection molding, and the mold was designed and analyzed using Moldflow CAE S/W. The optimal feedstock material was selected through comparison and analysis of three candidate materials. A mold was manufactured to test the injection molding process and evaluate related parameters. The resulting blade was assembled with other components, and a generator was installed to assess its durability, safety, and performance under various conditions. The results indicated the feasibility of producing a blade for a small wind turbine through injection molding, which predicted higher productivity and lower costs compared to traditional manufacturing methods that rely heavily on manual labor.

Title: Numerically and Experimentally Verified Design of a Small Wind Turbine with Injection Molded Blade
Snippet: According to the direction of the rotating axis relative to the wind direction, wind turbines are commonly classified as horizontal axis wind turbine (HAWT) and vertical axis wind turbine (VAWT). AWM-750D is a novel wind turbine model based on the Archimedes wind turbine series, a type of HAWT, under development. It contains blades of diameter 0.75 m and rated power of 100 W at 12.5 m/s of wind speed. The turbine blades are spiral-shaped, which is unique compared with those of conventional wind turbines and is registered as a patent, WO 2014/073741 A1 [23]. 

The power generating part of wind turbines is composed of three blades rotating around a shaft. We manufactured the blade via injection molding instead of rolling and stretching it in an axial direction due to the advantages of structural robustness, quality, and productivity. Figure 1 depicts the development background and major components of the system. We placed a generator upstream of the rotating part and a brake downstream to attain dynamic stability. Moreover, it can direct automatically toward the upcoming wind by drag, which is advantageous for drag-type wind turbines. The household small wind turbine system is aimed for installation and operation in urban environments, and it is crucial to enhance the operability for competitiveness in the market. The authors [24] analyzed that small wind turbines operating in the city possessed low operability due to uneven and low-speed wind and various buildings and obstacles. Therefore, many studies have stressed the importance of a light-weight and highly efficient blade design. 

Plastic injection molding, which is used for manufacturing turbine blades of a unique shape with spirals, is one of the most complex and challenging processes. Here, polymers are formed whilst hot (or plastic) having large and complex molecules. The size variation, entanglement, and orientation affect the material behavior. During the plastic state, polymers act as non-Newtonian viscoelastic fluids. When formed and in use, they are greatly affected by time and temperature. This complex range of attributes signifies that simple classical design theories are ineffective or dangerous. The injection molding process contains many variables such as the polymer type, melt temperature, injection pressure and rate, mold temperature, gate size, gate position, feed geometry, injection profiles, etc.

Title: Aspects Regarding the Use of 3D Printing Technology and Composite Materials for Testing and Manufacturing Vertical Axis Wind Turbines
Snippet: 3D printing (3DP), specifically fused filament fabrication (FFF), is one of the most accessible and widespread rapid prototyping technologies [1][2][3][4][5][6][7]. Recent advances in additive manufacturing (AM), a construction technique where a three-dimensional object is created through the build-up of thin layers of a thermoplastic material, have resulted in the commercialization and popularization of what is commonly known as 3DP. [1][2][3][4][6][7][8] Objects for 3D printing are stored in digital files for modification using 3D modeling software, and are easily copied, and transferred via the Internet. Small wind turbine technology stands to benefit greatly from this technology. With the appropriate design, wind turbines could be rapidly manufactured (printed) and assembled on-site at an as needed basis without too many tools beyond a 3D printing machine and printing filament, or at least it helps a lot in creating the complicated geometry of wind turbine blades that would be quite difficult to produce with other technologies.

Title: Design and Optimisation of Horizontal Axis Wind Turbine Blades Using Biomimicry of Whale Tubercles
Snippet: In horizontal-axis wind turbines, a lift is generated by the airfoil geometry of the turbine blades (HAWT). The biggest issue, though, is the likelihood of blade stalls after a certain angle of attack. According to the literature, tubercles, and other devices can improve momentum transfer in wind turbine blades and hence increase lift generation. Concurrently, these changes assist in delaying the stalling of the blade. This study examines the various alterations made to the leading edge of the HAWT blade using tubercles, as well as their implications on aerodynamic performance. The following major findings about the performance of HAWT with leading-edge tubercles are summarized: (i) blades with tubercles on the leading edge will have superior performance in the post-stall regime, (ii) tubercles with a smaller amplitude and lower wavelength will produce higher lift and lower drag in the low wind speed condition, and (iii) tubercle blade will have a stable and smooth performance in varying wind speed conditions, producing higher torque and power at low wind speed. 

These findings will, later on, be tested and confirmed with CAD software. The results of these tests will bring some crucial scopes for future research for further developing the HAWT with tubercle blades delineated.

Title: Dynamic stall on airfoils with leading-edge tubercles
Snippet: This suggests that tubercles effectively act as dynamic stall mitigation devices, reducing the intensity and duration of lift overshoots, thereby enhancing overall aerodynamic stability during dynamic stall conditions. This can be especially beneficial for airfoils operating in a wide range of conditions, such as wind turbine blades and helicopter rotors, which regularly experience dynamic stall. In these applications, minimizing lift hysteresis and reducing cyclic structural loads can significantly improve performance and durability.

Title: Design and Optimisation of Horizontal Axis Wind Turbine Blades Using Biomimicry of Whale Tubercles
Snippet: Wind speed is the major factor in generating power in a wind turbine. In the present study, modifications were done on the leading edge of the HAWT blade using tubercles showing their effects on aerodynamic performances. Using a small wind turbine model, SolidWorks Motion Analysis Simulation was used for dynamic modeling to evaluate and determine the force and torque of the mechanical structure. Title: Effect of protuberances on the aerodynamic performance of a wind turbine blade – a review
Snippet: The opposite trend was reported in the post-stall regime. The use of protuberances was beneficial for power generation, especially at low and unsteady wind speeds. Arunvinthan, Pillai, and Cao (2020) reported that the protuberances help improve the lift coefficient and decrease the flow separation tendency at higher AoA. The experimental studies were performed on small, medium and high LEPs of a wind turbine blade. The abrupt type stall inception was transformed into the progressive type after incorporating the medium and high LEPs. The small LEP was found to have negligible influence on the stall characteristics of the blade. Sudhakar, Karthikeyan, and Venkatakrishnan (2017) investigated the effect of tubercles on blade performance and reported that the addition of tubercles improved the stability of the system and eliminated the hysteresis in the pitching moment. This performance improvement substantially helps during the sudden vertical gusts. Shi, Atlar, and Norman (2017) used the Stereo Particle Image Velocimetry technique and showed that the presence of tubercles weakens the tip leakage vortex, leading to a substantial reduction in the axial trajectory. snippet.text:
In horizontal-axis wind turbines, a lift is generated by the airfoil geometry of the turbine blades (HAWT). The biggest issue, though, is the likelihood of blade stalls after a certain angle of attack. According to the literature, tubercles, and other devices can improve momentum transfer in wind turbine blades and hence increase lift generation. Concurrently, these changes assist in delaying the stalling of the blade. This study examines the various alterations made to the leading edge of the HAWT blade using tubercles, as well as their implications on aerodynamic performance. The following major findings about the performance of HAWT with leading-edge tubercles are summarized: (i) blades with tubercles on the leading edge will have superior performance in the post-stall regime, (ii) tubercles with a smaller amplitude and lower wavelength will produce higher lift and lower drag in the low wind speed condition, and (iii) tubercle blade will have a stable and smooth performance in varying wind speed conditions, producing higher torque and power at low wind speed. 

These findings will, later on, be tested and confirmed with CAD software. The results of these tests will bring some crucial scopes for future research for further developing the HAWT with tubercle blades delineated.
